records.name: Ad-Hoc Endpoints

distinctFrom.reason: Ad-hoc endpoints are inconsistent one-off shapes, while a chatty interface is one operation needing many small calls.

records.definition: Exposing inconsistent, one-off endpoints instead of a uniform interface, forcing clients to special-case each.

records.name: Ad-Hoc Payloads
records.definition: Sending payloads with no agreed schema, so consumers must guess at structure and break on change.

records.name: Breaking API Change
records.definition: Changing an API in a way that violates its published contract, breaking existing clients.

records.name: Breaking Change
records.definition: A change that violates a component's contract, forcing consumers to update to keep working.

records.name: External State Mutation
records.definition: Mutating state outside an object's own boundary, breaking the invariants it is supposed to guarantee.

records.name: Hidden Service Coupling
records.definition: An undeclared dependency between services that surfaces only at runtime, undermining independent evolution.

records.name: Implementation-First Integration
records.definition: Integrating against a concrete implementation before agreeing a contract, coupling consumers to internals.

records.name: Implicit Assumptions
records.definition: Relying on unstated preconditions a caller must satisfy, which break silently when they are violated.

records.name: Implicit Behavior
records.definition: Behavior a component performs that is not stated in its contract, surprising callers who come to depend on it.

records.name: Proprietary Coupling
records.definition: Binding to a vendor's proprietary interface, forfeiting interoperability and portability.

records.name: Proprietary Drift
records.definition: Extending a standard protocol with proprietary features until it no longer interoperates with others.

records.name: Silent Breaking Changes
records.definition: Shipping a breaking change with no version bump or notice, so consumers fail without warning.

records.name: Strict Fragile Parsers
records.definition: Parsers that reject any input deviating from an exact expectation, breaking on benign additions.

records.name: Undefined Results
records.definition: Returning results a contract never specifies for a given input, leaving callers with undefined behavior.

records.name: Compatibility Policy
records.definition: The declared rules governing which changes are compatible and how versions are managed.

records.name: Consistent Semantics

distinctFrom.reason: Consistent semantics is one meaning across resources, while stable contracts are one shape over time.

records.definition: The requirement that the same operation mean the same thing across every resource and endpoint.

records.name: Extensible Schema
records.definition: A schema shaped so new fields can be added without breaking existing consumers.

records.name: Protocol Contract
records.definition: The agreed rules of a protocol, such as its messages, formats and sequences, that both ends must honor.

records.name: Result Validation
records.definition: The activity of checking that an operation's result satisfies its promised postconditions.

records.name: Semantic Contract
records.definition: An agreement specifying not just the shape of an interface but the meaning and behavior it guarantees.

records.name: API Usability
records.definition: The degree to which an API is easy for developers to learn and use correctly.

records.name: Automated Validation
records.definition: The ability to check data automatically against a declared schema.

records.name: Client Compatibility
records.definition: The degree to which existing clients continue to work as an API evolves.

records.name: Consumer-Driven Development
records.definition: The ability to shape a provider's contract from the concrete needs of its consumers.

records.name: Consumer-Verified Compatibility
records.definition: The ability to verify a provider still satisfies the contracts its consumers depend on.

records.name: Contract Testing
records.definition: The activity of testing that an implementation honors the contract it declares.

records.name: Cross-System Communication
records.definition: The ability for independent systems to exchange and understand data with one another.

records.name: Incremental Deployment
records.definition: The ability to roll out changes gradually while old and new versions coexist.

records.name: Independent Consumers
records.definition: The ability for consumers to evolve on their own schedule because the interface stays stable.

records.name: Multi-Client Integration
records.definition: The ability to serve many different clients through one compatible protocol.

records.name: Provider Change Safety
records.definition: The degree to which a provider can change without breaking its consumers, verified by their contracts.

records.name: Reliable Integration
records.definition: The degree to which systems integrate correctly because their shared meaning is agreed, not just their shape.

records.name: Rolling Upgrades
records.definition: The ability to upgrade instances one at a time while old and new versions interoperate.

records.name: Schema Evolution
records.definition: The ability to change a data schema over time without breaking existing readers or writers.

records.name: Consumer Safety
records.definition: The degree to which consumers are protected from breakage when a provider changes.

records.name: Data Quality
records.definition: The degree to which data is accurate, complete, and fit for its intended use.

records.name: Integration
records.definition: The degree to which separate systems are connected to operate as a unified whole.

records.name: Cleanup / Simplification
records.definition: The activity of removing obsolete code and structure, which backward compatibility can hold back.

records.name: Cross-Domain Translation
records.definition: The activity of mapping terms and structures between two domains that model the world differently.

records.name: Development Speed
records.definition: The rate at which new functionality is built, which upfront contract rigor can slow.

records.name: Distributed Evolution
records.definition: The degree to which services can evolve independently, constrained by the contracts binding them.

records.name: Domain-Specific Optimization
records.definition: The degree to which a system is tuned for one domain, traded against broad interoperability.

records.name: Evolution
records.definition: The ability to change an interface over time, in tension with the stability its contract promises.

records.name: Evolution Speed
records.definition: The rate at which an interface can change, which a commitment to stability deliberately limits.

records.name: Flexibility
records.definition: The degree to which a component permits varied use, in tension with the invariants it must uphold.

records.name: Flexible Ingestion
records.definition: The degree to which a system accepts loosely-structured input, in tension with a strict data contract.

records.name: Interface Overuse
records.definition: The degree to which excessive interface abstraction adds indirection without proportional benefit.

records.name: Permissive APIs
records.definition: The degree to which an API accepts loose or lenient input, in tension with strict preconditions.

records.name: Protocol Optimization
records.definition: The degree to which a protocol is tuned for performance, traded against broad compatibility.

records.name: Provider Autonomy
records.definition: The degree of freedom a provider retains to change, constrained by consumer-driven contracts.

records.name: Rapid Prototyping
records.definition: The activity of building quick throwaway prototypes, which explicit contracts can slow.

records.name: Runtime Cost
records.definition: The degree of runtime overhead incurred by checking conditions on every call.

records.name: Schema Flexibility
records.definition: The degree to which a schema tolerates variation, in tension with a strict contract.

records.name: Specialized Endpoints
records.definition: The degree to which purpose-built endpoints are offered, traded against a uniform interface.

records.name: Strong Validation
records.definition: The degree to which input is strictly validated, in tension with tolerating unknown future fields.

records.name: Version Sprawl
records.definition: The degree to which many concurrent versions accumulate and must be maintained.

records.name: Standard Error Contract
records.definition: A technique for giving every error one published shape with a code, a message and its context.

records.name: Introduce Boundary DTO
records.definition: A technique for carrying data across a boundary in a transfer object, so internal models stay inside.

records.name: Coarse-Grained Endpoint
records.definition: A technique for serving one client operation with one call that returns everything the operation needs.

records.name: Backward-Compatible Change
records.definition: A technique for changing a contract only by additions that existing consumers can ignore.

records.name: Compatibility Adapter
records.definition: A technique for serving an old contract through an adapter over the new one while consumers migrate.

records.name: Gradual Deprecation
records.definition: A technique for announcing a removal with a date, warning the consumers still using it, and removing it after the date.

records.name: Migration Guide
records.definition: A technique for publishing the steps a consumer takes to move from one version of a contract to the next.

records.name: Version Bump
records.definition: A technique for raising a contract's version number by the rule that says which kind of change it carries.

records.name: Consumer-Driven Contract Tests
records.definition: A technique for having each consumer publish the responses it relies on and testing the provider against all of them before it releases.

records.name: Define Contract
records.definition: A technique for publishing the operations, shapes and guarantees of a boundary before implementing either side of it.

records.name: Standardize the Interface
records.definition: A technique for giving operations of one kind the same naming, shapes and conventions across a system.

records.name: Tolerant Reader
records.definition: A technique for reading only the fields a consumer needs and ignoring unknown ones, so additive changes do not break it.
